h1: Guest posting vs digital PR: count the links still live a year later
metaTitle: Guest Posting vs Digital PR: Links After a Year
metaDescription: Guest posting vs digital PR, scored on links still live after 12 months. We compare 20 placements against one data story pitched to the Indian press.
answer: Score both on links still live after twelve months, not links placed. ₹1 lakh buys roughly 15–25 guest posts at Indian market rates, or one original-data story pitched to business media. The guest posts decay page by page; the PR story decays too, but it also produces brand mentions and pickups guest posts never generate.
takeaways: Links placed is a vanity number. Links still live, still indexed and still on a page with readers, twelve months later — that's the number.
Guest post inventory churns. Sites get sold, pruned, blanket-nofollowed or quietly deindexed, and nobody emails you when it happens.
Indian business desks want a number with a source. They will not run your product launch.
Google's own spam policies name large-scale article campaigns. That's not a rumour, it's published guidance.

sections.h2: Count the links twice: once on delivery, once in a year
body: Every link-building proposal is scored on placements. Twenty links, DA 40+, delivered in 30 days. Clean number, fits a spreadsheet, measures the wrong moment.

The number that matters is how many of those links are still live twelve months later — still indexed, still on a domain that exists and has an audience. That's the asset you paid for. Everything before it is inventory.
So here's the comparison run properly: the same ₹1 lakh, spent both ways, scored at month twelve rather than month one.

One honesty note first. We have no published survival study to cite, and neither does anyone else selling you either service — so what follows is a planning model with its assumptions stated out loud, not a measured result. Treat any agency quoting a precise decay percentage with the suspicion it deserves.
At Indian market rates, ₹1 lakh buys very different-shaped things depending on which door you walk through.

table.caption: The same ₹1 lakh month. Twelve-month figures are planning assumptions with reasoning, not measured data.
head: ₹1 lakh on guest posts
₹1 lakh on one data story
rows: What it buys
Roughly 15–25 placements at ₹4,000–₹7,000 each, on low-to-mid authority sites sold through marketplaces and WhatsApp groups.
One original-data asset: the data work, the analysis, the write-up, a designer, and a pitch list of 30–60 named journalists.
Delivery
2–5 weeks, near-certain. You're buying a slot.
6–10 weeks, no certainty. Execute perfectly and get two pickups, or twenty.
Anchor text control
Complete. Which is exactly the problem.
Zero. Journalists link how they want, or to your homepage, or not at all.
Referral traffic
Usually negligible. These pages don't have readers.
Real but spiky, concentrated in the first fortnight.
Pickups and mentions
None. Nobody syndicates a guest post, and a byline nobody reads isn't a mention.
The main reason to do it. One desk running your number leads others to cite and repeat it, in publications your buyers already read.
Risk under Google's policies
Named directly in the link spam policies as large-scale article campaigns.
None. This is the behaviour the policies were written to reward.
What we plan for at 12 months
Assume a meaningful share are gone or worthless — sites sold, posts pruned, outbound blanket-nofollowed, domains deindexed. We budget as if a third to a half won't be doing anything.
The article usually survives; major publishers don't delete archives. Its traffic decays, the citation and the brand association don't.

callout.title: The asymmetry nobody puts in the proposal
callout.body: Guest posting has certain output and uncertain value. Digital PR has uncertain output and certain value if it lands. Most founders buy the certain output — a preference for a comfortable invoice, not a better asset.

sections.h2: Why guest-post links decay and news links mostly don't
body: Nothing dramatic causes this. Six ordinary things do, and none of them generate an email telling you it happened.
bullets: **The site gets sold.** Marketplace inventory changes hands constantly. New owner, new outbound policy, or a wholesale content purge.
**The post gets pruned.** Owners doing a content cleanup delete the sponsored archive first, because they know what it is.
**Outbound links get blanket-nofollowed.** One theme setting, applied site-wide, and every link you bought becomes a [nofollow link](/compare/dofollow-vs-nofollow) overnight.
**The domain gets deindexed.** A site publishing eight sponsored posts a day across unrelated categories is a candidate, and when it goes, everything on it goes.
**The page rots.** Still live, no internal links, no traffic, no reason for Google to recrawl it. Technically a link. Functionally furniture.
**Hosting lapses.** Small sites just stop existing.

callout.title: The one advantage guest posts have
callout.body: You control the URL you link to and the anchor. On a PR pickup you get whatever the journalist writes — often your homepage, sometimes no link at all. If you need a specific page supported, PR is a blunt instrument.

sections.h2: What an Indian business desk will actually run
body: Most digital PR fails in India for a boring reason: the pitch has no number in it.

Economic Times, Business Standard, Mint, Moneycontrol, Financial Express, BusinessLine, and on the startup side Inc42, Entrackr and YourStory — they run stories, not announcements. A story needs something the reporter can't get elsewhere, expressed as a figure, with a named source and a stated method.

The cheat code most Indian companies miss is that they already own the data. Your booking system knows what people order and when. Your marketplace account knows which pin codes buy what. That's original data, it costs nothing, and it beats any survey you could commission for ₹1 lakh.

bullets: Category or state-level numbers nobody else has: what a segment paid, ordered, searched or cancelled, broken out by city or month.
Salary, hiring and attrition data with a stated sample and method.
Price movement in a category people feel — food, gold, rent, freight, tuition.
A genuine reversal: what everyone assumes, contradicted by your own numbers, with the numbers attached.
Timing. The same data pitched in budget week beats it pitched in a random fortnight.
Product launches, funding-adjacent hints, and "we're excited to announce".
Surveys with an undisclosed sample size. Desks that care will ask; the ones that don't ask are the ones you didn't want.
Opinion pieces from a founder nobody has heard of yet.
Anything where the story is your company rather than your data.

callout.title: Expect nofollow, and take it anyway
callout.body: Plenty of Indian publications nofollow outbound commercial links, link only to your homepage, or name you with no link at all. Still the better outcome. A named mention in a paper your buyers read does work a marketplace guest post cannot, and Google has treated nofollow as a hint since March 2020.

sections.h2: Google's actual position on guest posting at scale
body: This gets misquoted in both directions, so here's the published position rather than the folklore.

Google's spam policies name **large-scale article campaigns** — guest posts, advertorials and syndicated articles produced primarily to place keyword-rich links — as link spam. Google has also said repeatedly that links in guest posts should carry `nofollow`, because the author has an interest in the link.

What Google has *not* said is that guest posting is banned. A contributed article by someone with real expertise, on a publication with a real audience, that would exist even if the link didn't — that's normal publishing and always has been.

The line is intent and scale, and both are visible from outside. Twenty placements in a month, on unrelated sites, with commercial anchors, from a domain that had no links in the month before, is a legible pattern — and link spam systems are pattern-matchers.

The consequence usually isn't a penalty. It's quieter: the links get devalued, you've spent ₹1 lakh, nothing happens, and no report tells you why. What that looks like in practice is in [paid links vs earned links](/compare/paid-links-vs-earned-links).

sections.h2: The thing guest posts never produce: a mention
body: A link is a signal about a page. A mention is a signal about a company, and they don't do the same job.

When a business paper names you, several things happen that no guest post produces. Your buyers see it — some are reading that paper the same morning. Your sales team gets a line for the deck. Your next pitch is easier, because you're now a source somebody has quoted. And search engines accumulate an association between your brand name and a category, on a page they trust.

That last one has become materially more valuable. AI answers work from text, not link attributes. Being described accurately, in the right category, on a crawled page, is now part of how you appear in a result with no blue links in it at all.
A byline on a site with no readers produces none of that. It produces a row in a backlink tool. Different products, sold at similar prices.
We're not absolutists about this. There's a real case where guest posting is the correct answer.

If you sell something the business press will never cover — industrial fasteners, a niche compliance tool, a component that goes inside somebody else's product — then the trade publication, the practitioner blog and the association newsletter *are* your media. A contributed technical article there isn't link spam. It's the only distribution that exists.

The test is easy to apply. Would you write this article if the link were nofollowed and that site were the only place your buyers read? If yes, write it. If the article exists to hold the link, you're buying inventory, and the twelve-month scoreboard will say so.
For budget context, see [what link building costs in India](/cost/link-building-cost) and how we structure [digital PR work](/services/digital-pr-services).

versus.verdict: For a company with something countable to say, put the ₹1 lakh into one original-data story — it survives longer and produces brand mentions guest posts never do; guest posting only wins when your buyers read trade publications the business press will never cover.

faqs.q: Is guest posting still effective in 2026?
faqs.a: As publishing, yes. As a link tactic bought in bulk, it's the pattern Google's spam policies describe as large-scale article campaigns. The practical test: would you write the article if the link were nofollowed? If yes it's publishing, if no it's inventory, and inventory is what gets devalued.

faqs.q: How much does digital PR cost in India?
faqs.a: A modest data-led story runs around ₹1 lakh in effort when you already own the data, and considerably more when you have to commission a survey. Ongoing PR retainers sit higher. The variance is large because you're buying attempts, not placements — nobody can price a guaranteed pickup honestly.

faqs.q: How do I pitch an Indian business journalist?
faqs.a: Short email, subject line that is the number, three sentences of finding, one line on method and sample, and the full data attached or linked. Name the desk correctly. Offer an exclusive if the data warrants it. Don't attach a press release and don't follow up more than once.

faqs.q: What if the publication nofollows the link or doesn't link at all?
faqs.a: Take it. Nofollow has been a hint rather than a rule since March 2020, and the named brand mention on a page your buyers and search engines both read does work a followed marketplace link can't. If you need a specific page supported, that's a job for internal linking, not PR.

faqs.q: Can I do both in the same month?
faqs.a: You can, and on ₹1 lakh you'll do neither well. A data story needs the whole budget to be worth pitching, and a half-sized guest post run buys the same risk at a smaller scale. Pick one per quarter and score it properly at month twelve.

faqs.q: How do I know if my old guest post links are still live?
faqs.a: Export your referring domains, then crawl the specific linking URLs monthly and check three things: does the page still return 200, is your link still in the HTML, and has a `rel` attribute appeared. Almost nobody does this, which is why link decay stays invisible.
